lesson.text: Quick memory: in one-point perspective, where do the lines going away from you meet? (At the vanishing point, on the horizon.) Today: two vanishing points.
Look at a building from its corner, not face on. Now both its sides go away from you, each to its own vanishing point. That is two-point perspective.
Draw the horizon at your eye level and put a vanishing point near each end. Then draw the nearest corner, the leading edge, as an upright line.
From the top and the bottom of the leading edge, draw lines to both vanishing points. Upright lines stay upright: they never go to a vanishing point.
Choose where each side ends with two more upright lines. Then rub out the parts of the guide lines you do not need.
A box below the horizon shows its top, as if you look down on it; above the horizon you see its underside, like a tall building. Across the horizon you see neither.
Worked example: a house. Draw the corner, send its top and bottom to both points, add the far edges, then a roof. Windows and doors shrink towards their wall's vanishing point too.
Try it in the world: stand at the corner of a building in your world. See how the lines of its roof and base slope away to the left and to the right. Next: expression and emotion.

exercises.hint: It sits on the horizon, and lines run to it.
exercises.explain: It is a vanishing point: the box's right side goes back to it.

exercises.prompt: In two-point perspective, upright lines stay upright.
exercises.explain: True: only lines going back run to the vanishing points.

exercises.prompt: How many vanishing points does two-point perspective have?
exercises.explain: Two: one for each side of the box.

exercises.prompt: What is the marked line called?
exercises.hint: It is the nearest corner, drawn first.
exercises.explain: It is the leading edge: the nearest corner, drawn as an upright line.

exercises.prompt: Label the drawing (VP means vanishing point): tap a word, then its number.
exercises.hint: The VPs are the dots at the ends of the horizon; the near edge is the box's front corner.
exercises.explain: The dots at each end of the eye-level line are the left and right VPs, the line is the horizon, and the front corner is the near (leading) edge.

exercises.prompt: Where is this box, compared with the horizon?
exercises.hint: Can you see the top of the box?
choices: below it: we see its top
above it: we see its underside
exercises.explain: It is below the horizon, so we look down and see its top.

exercises.prompt: Why can you see the underside of this box?
exercises.hint: Where is the horizon: above or below the box?
exercises.explain: It is above the horizon, so we look up at it and see its underside.

exercises.prompt: The horizon is always drawn at the top of the page.
exercises.explain: False: it is at your eye level, wherever that is in the picture.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps of drawing a box in two-point perspective in order.
exercises.hint: You need the horizon before the points, and the corner before the lines.
items: put a vanishing point near each end
add the far edges and rub out
exercises.explain: Horizon, two points, the leading edge, lines to both points, then the far edges.

exercises.hint: How many sides go away from you?
choices: a building seen from its corner
a flat wall seen face on
exercises.explain: From a corner, two sides go away, so you need two points.

exercises.prompt: Label this drawing (VP means vanishing point).
exercises.hint: The VPs sit on the horizon, high up here; the near edge is the front corner.
exercises.explain: The dots on the high horizon are the left and right VPs; the box's front corner is the near edge.

exercises.prompt: Windows along a wall in two-point perspective get smaller towards that wall's vanishing point.
exercises.explain: True: they are further away, so they shrink towards the point.

exercises.prompt: Zara draws a tall tower as she sees it from the ground. Where should her horizon go?
exercises.hint: The horizon is at eye level. Where are her eyes?
exercises.explain: Her eyes are near the ground, so the horizon is low and she looks up at the tower.

exercises.prompt: What happens to lines that go straight up in two-point perspective?
exercises.hint: Look at the box's three corners.
choices: they go to the left point
they go to the right point
exercises.explain: They stay upright; only lines going back meet at the points.

exercises.prompt: What are the dashed grey lines?
exercises.hint: Follow them to where they end.
choices: guide lines to the vanishing points
exercises.explain: They are guide lines from the box's corners to the vanishing points.

exercises.prompt: If the two vanishing points are very close together, the box looks stretched and odd.
exercises.explain: True: points far apart give a natural look; close points bend it out of shape.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to what it means.
matches: a line at your eye level
exercises.hint: The leading edge is the corner nearest to you.
exercises.explain: The horizon is at your eye level, lines going away meet at a vanishing point, and the leading edge is the nearest upright corner.

exercises.prompt: A house in two-point perspective: sort its lines. Upright, or to a vanishing point?
items: the top of the left wall
the bottom of the right wall
exercises.hint: Upright lines stay upright. Lines along a wall go back to that wall's point.
exercises.explain: Upright: the leading edge, a door's sides and the far corners. To a vanishing point: the tops and bottoms of the walls, and the top of a window, which all run back along a wall.

exercises.prompt: Match each choice in a two-point drawing to its effect.
matches: you look up at a tall tower
you look down on the town
exercises.hint: The horizon is your eye level. Where are your eyes? How far apart should the points be?
exercises.explain: A low horizon puts your eyes near the ground, so you look up. A high horizon means you look down. Points far apart look natural; points close together stretch the box out of shape.
